USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We are three days from the December 15 tariff deadline on ~$156-160 billion of Chinese consumer goods, with a Phase One deal announced only 'in principle' (Oct 11) and still unsigned. We should finalize and sign that deal now: convert the reported plan to delay the December 15 tariffs into a signed agreement that locks in the $40-50 billion agricultural purchase framework, IP/financial-services commitments, and the currency pact, while keeping existing tariffs on ~$360 billion of Chinese goods in place as leverage for Phase Two. We should formally announce the December 15 deferral as part of that signing, not before, so we preserve maximum negotiating leverage. Do not overreach with further escalation, but also do not trade away the credible threat still embedded in the existing tariff schedule.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat environment does not justify a defensive or crisis posture. US macro data at the decision date show an economy absorbing the trade war well: consumer sentiment has rebounded from its 89.8 August trough to 99.3 in December, the Fed has cut the funds rate to 1.55%, 10-year yields have stabilized near 1.79%, Baa corporate spreads are tight at 3.83%, and oil is benign near $58. The drag is real but contained and known: industrial production is flat, and the farm belt is in a genuine recession, with two rounds of taxpayer assistance already paid out and China slow-walking confirmation of the promised purchases (Beijing has never confirmed the $40-50B figure). That asymmetry is why the threat reads mildly negative (opportunistic) rather than neutral: the US sits on the escalation side of every remaining lever, the trade deficit with China is falling more than 10% this year, and the other side is under duress from a decelerating economy. The action stance is negotiation, not concession: delaying the December 15 tariffs in exchange for a signed text is not a concession but the capstone of the current strategy, and reports the administration is already preparing exactly this deferral confirm it is the low-risk path. The risk to manage is execution risk, not counterparty strength - China has not yet delivered a written commitment on the headline purchase numbers, and the Hong Kong Human Rights Act signing adds a parallel track of friction that must not be allowed to contaminate the trade channel. Signing Phase One to a first-step deadline, with the December 15 hike already deferred, hard-wires the result most favorable to the American economy while retaining ~$360 billion of tariff headroom for the next round.
key_factors: US economy resilient at decision date: consumer sentiment 99.3 (rebound from 89.8 Aug trough), Fed cuts to 1.55%, 10Y ~1.79%, tight Baa spreads
Phase One deal (Oct 11) announced only 'in principle' - $40-50B ag, IP, FX - but unsigned; China has never confirmed the headline purchase figures
Dec 15 deadline on ~$156-160B of List 4B consumer goods is 3 days away; Dec 10 reporting indicates administration plans to delay it
US holds escalation leverage: ~$360B of existing tariffs retained, trade deficit with China falling >10% in 2019
Risks: farm economy in recession (two rounds of assistance paid), industrial production flat, Hong Kong Human Rights Act adds non-trade friction, two prior truces (Buenos Aires, Osaka) collapsed
Oil benign (~$58) and easy financial conditions limit systemic stress from further escalation

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and continue negotiating the Phase One deal without making new unilateral concessions, while preserving our core demand that the US roll back tariffs as part of any settlement. We should engage constructively to keep the deal alive and avoid forcing the US's pending Dec 15 tariffs (List 4B) onto nearly all remaining Chinese exports, using our existing goodwill signals (waived soy/pork duties, exemption lists) as our leverage rather than escalating. Do not concede on tariff rollback or accept a one-sided purchases-only deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but not existential. China's November exports fell 1.1% YoY for the fourth straight month, with exports to the US down 23% and 12 straight monthly declines (Reuters/BBC, Dec 8), while GDP growth cooled to 6% in Q3, near 30-year lows (AP). Firm-level targeting persists: Huawei remains on the US Entity List since May 16, and Google/Android access was suspended (timeline May 16/20), directly threatening our tech-goals. That justifies a positive threat score near the +0.5 'major export sectors hit / firm-level targeting' anchor. However, it is not existential: the economy has been 'unexpectedly resilient,' imports rose for the first time since April on stimulus (Reuters Dec 8), and we hold asymmetric leverage (rare-earth signal, May 20; unreliable-entity list, May 31) plus diversification (EU exports +4.5%, ASEAN +11.5%). The trajectory is toward de-escalation: a Phase One deal was announced in principle Oct 11, and by Dec 10 reports indicate both sides are 'laying the groundwork' to delay the Dec 15 tariffs (CNBC/WSJ). Escalating now would be self-defeating — it would invite the Dec 15 tariffs onto virtually all remaining exports and deepen the export pain that is already our main vulnerability. Negotiating (action_score +0.2) captures that: engage to secure a deal and avoid new tariffs, hold firm on tariff rollback, and let the opponent's own need to avoid pre-Christmas tariffs work in our favor.
key_factors: China exports fell 4 straight months; US-bound exports down 23% YoY, 12 straight monthly declines
Huawei still on US Entity List; Google/Android suspended — tech-threat to CCP self-sufficiency goals
GDP growth cooled to 6% in Q3, near 30-year lows; imports recovering on stimulus (first rise since April)
Phase One deal announced in principle Oct 11 but unsigned for ~2 months; Dec 15 List 4B tariffs loom
Both sides reportedly laying groundwork to delay Dec 15 tariffs (CNBC/WSJ Dec 10)
China holds leverage: rare-earth signal, unreliable-entity list, diversification to EU/ASEAN
